units.subject: biology
units.decision_hinge: Decide which details belong in a scientific model for the question being asked.
units.mechanism: A useful scientific model simplifies a real system by keeping details that affect the question and ignoring details that do not affect it.

mx.cwo: An equation for the time of one orbit is not a model of the solar system; only a small ball-and-stick copy that looks like the real thing is a model.
There is one correct model of the human heart, so the same labelled diagram answers a question about blood flow and a question about heart muscle.
Air resistance is always ignored in physics, so a sheet of paper and a coin released together in the classroom reach the floor at the same instant.
In a model of a cricket ball in flight the bright red colour must be kept because it is the most noticeable thing about the ball, while the ball's mass can be left out.

units.subject: biology
units.decision_hinge: Decide whether a scientific word or symbol should be interpreted by its precise scientific meaning rather than its everyday meaning.
units.mechanism: Science uses language carefully: familiar words can have specific scientific meanings, and symbols may follow historical or international conventions rather than convenient abbreviations.

mx.cwo: The weight of the school bag is 5 kg, and it will still weigh 5 kg on the Moon.
The sentence 'the prisoner escaped from his cell' is scientifically wrong, because a cell is the basic unit of life.
The symbol for oxygen cannot be O, because chemical symbols never come from the English name of the element.
CO is the symbol for cobalt, because both letters of cobalt appear in it.
Sodium's symbol is So and potassium's is Po, taking the first two letters of each English name.

units.subject: biology
units.decision_hinge: Decide whether an equation is being used as a relationship between quantities, not just as a calculation to perform.
units.mechanism: Mathematics in science is a language for expressing relationships between quantities clearly and testing them carefully.

mx.cwo: In F = ma, taking m = 500 g and a = 2 m/s^2 gives F = 1000 N.
Beauty = kindness x 2 is a scientific equation, because it is written in symbols with an equals sign.
In a = F/m, doubling the mass doubles the acceleration, because m appears in the formula.
v = s/t is the speed relationship and s = vt is a different relationship, about distance, so the two cannot be used on the same problem.
From density = mass / volume it follows that mass = density / volume, so a substance of density 2 g/cm3 filling 5 cm3 has a mass of 0.4 g.

units.subject: biology
units.decision_hinge: Decide whether measurements must use the same units and conversions everywhere for a comparison or calculation to be valid.
units.mechanism: Measurements are useful only when units have agreed meanings; using different units or wrong conversions can make a calculation wrong even if the arithmetic is performed.

mx.cwo: The aircraft needed 22300 kilograms of fuel, so pumping in 22300 litres of fuel meets the requirement exactly.
Adding 2 kilograms of flour to 500 grams of sugar gives 502 kilograms of mixture.
A 2 kilometre walk is shorter than a 900 metre walk, because 2 is a much smaller number than 900.
22300 pounds is close enough to 22300 kilograms for refuelling, since both are around twenty thousand and the estimate only needs the right scale.
To change 5 kilograms into grams, divide by 1000, so 5 kilograms is 0.005 grams.

units.subject: biology
units.decision_hinge: Decide whether an idea is a scientific law, a scientific theory, or an unsupported guess.
units.mechanism: In science, laws describe patterns, theories explain why patterns occur using evidence available at the time, and a scientific theory is not an untested guess.

mx.cwo: Newton's law of gravitation has been proved, so no new evidence could ever change it.
'Hot air rises' is a scientific law, because it is a short general statement that is always said in science class.
Newton's law of gravitation is a theory because it explains why things fall, and the kinetic theory of gases is a law because gases always behave that way.
Because scientific ideas can always change, the claim that the Earth is flat could still turn out to be right.

units.subject: biology
units.decision_hinge: Decide whether a prediction is scientific because it uses measurable evidence and reasoning rather than guesswork.
units.mechanism: A scientific prediction is strengthened when it is based on evidence, reasoning, measurable information, and past patterns.

mx.cwo: The prediction of rain is scientific because the television weather presenter is an expert and said it would rain.
It will rain today because the temperature is 31 degrees Celsius; that is a measurement, so the prediction is scientific.
It did rain that evening, so Varsha's guess from the dark clouds was a scientific prediction after all.
A prediction about which team will win tomorrow can never be scientific, because science only predicts what happens inside a laboratory.
Saying there is a 70 percent chance of rain is scientific, while saying rain is likely because the pressure has fallen sharply is not, since only the first one has a number in it.

units.subject: biology
units.decision_hinge: Decide whether a failed prediction shows a limit to the model or theory rather than a reason to reject science by opinion.
units.mechanism: Scientific predictions can fail when conditions are complex, new, or measured more precisely; mismatches with observation are used as evidence to improve ideas.

mx.cwo: The forecast was wrong because the weather scientist made a mistake in the calculation, not because the model has limits.
Newton's laws predicted the planets correctly for centuries, so they must predict the bending of light near the Sun equally well.
The thermometer must have been read wrongly, because the model said the temperature would reach 35 degrees.
Since weather forecasts often fail, an eclipse predicted for a date years ahead is just as likely to be wrong.
The forecast said 30 millimetres of rain and 28 millimetres fell, so the model failed and should be rejected.

units.subject: biology
units.decision_hinge: Decide how to test a popular claim by asking scientific questions about evidence, mechanism, and observable consequences.
units.mechanism: A claim should be checked by asking whether a known mechanism and observable evidence support it, not by accepting it because it is widely circulated.

mx.cwo: Food could possibly become harmful during an eclipse, and since nobody can prove it does not, the warning is supported.
Several people who ate during the eclipse fell ill that night, so eating during an eclipse does spoil food.
Nobody has explained to me how the Moon causes the tides, so that is just a popular belief like the eclipse warning.
An eclipse is a rare and dramatic event, so it must have powerful effects on the body and on food.
Science keeps changing its mind, so the eclipse food warning may turn out to be right and should be followed until it is disproved.

units.subject: biology
units.decision_hinge: Decide when a rough estimate is reasonable by choosing assumptions, combining quantities, and checking the scale of the answer.
units.mechanism: A rough estimate can be useful when the aim is a reasonable scale rather than an exact value, as long as the assumptions and quantities are checked for reasonableness.

mx.cwo: A person needs exactly 8640 litres of air a day, so a cylinder holding 8640 litres will last exactly one day.
About 22000 kilograms of fuel is good enough for the flight, since an estimate only needs to have the right scale.
8640 litres per day is a better estimate than about 9000 litres per day, because it has more digits and looks more accurate.
At 15 breaths per minute the daily total is 15 times 24, which is 360 breaths, so a person breathes about 180 litres of air a day.

units.subject: biology
units.decision_hinge: Decide whether a real-life problem needs ideas from several branches of science rather than only one branch.
units.mechanism: Many real problems are understood by combining ideas from physics, chemistry, biology, earth science, or other areas instead of treating science as isolated branches.

mx.cwo: A traffic jam has nothing to do with chemistry, because chemistry is about test tubes and there are no test tubes on the road.
Boiling water for tea needs physics, chemistry, biology, earth science and astronomy together, because every real problem needs all the branches.
The question mentions a plant, so it is a biology question and no chemistry or physics is involved in it.

units.subject: biology
units.decision_hinge: Decide whether science should be understood as a human process of curiosity, questioning, collaboration, and testing rather than as a list of facts.
units.mechanism: Science is a human activity shaped by curiosity, creativity, collaboration, careful questioning, observation, testing, and the organisation of ideas.

mx.cwo: Scientists work alone and keep their results secret until they are certain, and only then is the result science.
You cannot ask a scientific question until you have learnt all the facts about the topic, so questions come at the end of science and not at the start.
Watching birds in a park and recording what they eat is not science, because there is no laboratory or apparatus involved.

units.subject: biology
units.decision_hinge: Decide whether a statement agrees with classical cell theory.
units.mechanism: All living organisms are made up of one or more cells; the cell is the basic unit of structure and function; and all cells arise from pre-existing cells.

mx.cwo: New cells form at a wound when the protoplasm and fluid there collect together and organise themselves into cells.
Amoeba is not really an organism, because an organism has to be built out of many cells working together.
When skin is cut, the skin tissue makes fresh cells out of itself to fill the gap.
Cell theory covers plants and animals, but bacteria are too simple to be made of cells and are not covered by it.
Blood is a liquid that pours, so it is not made of cells; only solid parts such as muscle are made of cells.

units.subject: biology
units.decision_hinge: Decide which viewing tool is needed to observe a cell structure clearly.
units.mechanism: Cells are usually too small for the unaided eye, so microscopes use magnification and resolution to make cell structures visible; electron microscopes reveal finer cell details than light microscopes.

mx.cwo: A light microscope cannot show ribosomes only because its magnification is too low, so a stronger eyepiece on the same microscope would bring them into view.
A light microscope can show the internal structure of a ribosome provided the section is cut thin enough and stained well.
Onion peel cells cannot be seen in a school laboratory at all, because seeing any cell needs an electron microscope.
A chloroplast is drawn larger than a whole cheek cell in the book, so a chloroplast needs less magnification than a cheek cell.

units.subject: biology
units.decision_hinge: Calculate an estimated cell size from microscope field diameter and the number of cells across it.
units.mechanism: Estimated size of one onion peel cell equals the diameter of the visible field in micrometres divided by the number of cells along that diameter.

mx.cwo: 5 divided by 25 gives 0.2, so each onion peel cell is about 0.2 micrometres across.
About 300 cells can be seen in the field, so 5000 divided by 300 gives roughly 17 micrometres for each cell.
50 cells now fit across the same field instead of 25, so each cell must be about 400 micrometres, twice as large as before.
At the higher power the field is still 5000 micrometres, so counting 100 cells gives 50 micrometres for each cell.
The eyepiece is 10x and the objective 40x, so the cell size is 5000 divided by 400, which is 12.5 micrometres.
25 cells divided by 5000 micrometres gives 0.005, so each cell measures 0.005 micrometres.

units.subject: biology
units.decision_hinge: Decide what the cell membrane does in a living cell.
units.mechanism: The cell membrane is a thin, selectively permeable plasma membrane that surrounds a cell, protects its contents, defines its individuality, and helps substances pass through by means of its lipid and protein structure.

mx.cwo: The cell membrane is made of cellulose and gives the cell its rigid box shape.
Bacteria and plant cells have a cell wall, so they do not need a cell membrane as well.
In a plant cell the cellulose wall decides what gets in, so the membrane inside it does no gatekeeping at all.
The cell membrane is the thin line drawn round the diagram, so its job is only to show where the cell stops.
The cell membrane pulls water into the cell whenever the cell is short of water and pushes it out when there is too much.

units.subject: biology
units.decision_hinge: Predict whether a cell or tissue piece will swell, shrink, or stay about the same in a solution.
units.mechanism: Water movement by osmosis depends on the relative solute concentration inside and outside the cell: water entering causes swelling, and water leaving causes shrinkage.

mx.cwo: Any cell placed in salt solution loses water and shrinks, even when the cell sap is more concentrated than the solution outside.
A potato strip in concentrated sugar solution swells and gains weight, because water moves out of the sugar solution and into the strip.
A boiled potato strip left in plain water swells just as much as a fresh one, because osmosis is a physical rule that does not need a living cell.
The strip in syrup shrinks because syrup is thick and sticky and squeezes the water out of the tissue.
An onion cell in concentrated sugar solution loses no water at all, because the cellulose wall keeps the water locked inside.

units.subject: biology
units.decision_hinge: Decide whether an observed cell shape difference is explained by the presence of a cell wall.
units.mechanism: Plant cells have a rigid cell wall outside the cell membrane that maintains shape and helps withstand stress, while animal cells lack a cell wall and can shrink or change shape more easily.

mx.cwo: The cheek cell shrinks in salt solution because it has no cell membrane to hold its shape.
A plant cell in concentrated sugar solution neither loses water nor changes inside, because the cell wall stops water from leaving.
A bacterium looks round and smooth, so it has no cell wall; only cells with straight edges have walls.
Only plant cells have a cell wall, so a fungus or a bacterium has just a membrane around it.

units.subject: biology
units.decision_hinge: Classify a cell as prokaryotic or eukaryotic from its internal organization.
units.mechanism: Prokaryotic cells lack a well-defined nucleus and have genetic material in a nucleoid region, while eukaryotic cells such as plant and animal cells have a well-defined nucleus and membrane-bound organelles.

mx.cwo: A bacterial cell is eukaryotic, because its nucleoid is a nucleus that holds the DNA together in one place.
This cell has a cell wall, so it is a plant cell and therefore eukaryotic.
Amoeba is neither prokaryotic nor eukaryotic, because those words apply only to bacteria and to plant and animal cells.
Bacteria must be eukaryotic, because they build proteins and digest food, and those jobs need ribosomes, Golgi apparatus and lysosomes.

units.subject: biology
units.decision_hinge: Decide how the nucleus and genetic material explain inheritance and cell control.
units.mechanism: In eukaryotic cells, the nucleus contains chromosomes that carry information for inheritance; in prokaryotic cells, genetic material is present in the nucleoid instead of a well-defined nucleus.

mx.cwo: The nucleolus contains the chromosomes made of DNA that carry inherited information to the next generation.
Chromosomes can be seen as separate rod-shaped structures in every cell at any time you look at it.
Every human cell has a nucleus, so a mature red blood cell has one too, hidden underneath the haemoglobin.
Bacteria have no nucleus, so they carry no genetic material and cannot pass characters on to the next generation.

units.subject: biology
units.decision_hinge: Match eukaryotic organelles to synthesis, processing, transport, and clean-up jobs.
units.mechanism: Eukaryotic cells use organelles as coordinated working parts: ribosomes synthesize proteins, the endoplasmic reticulum acts as a manufacturing network, the Golgi apparatus packages and ships materials, and lysosomes break down unwanted or damaged materials.

mx.cwo: Lysosomes are the sites where proteins are synthesised in a eukaryotic cell.
Only ribosomes stuck to the endoplasmic reticulum make proteins; the free ones floating in the cytoplasm are spare parts.
The Golgi apparatus makes the proteins and sends them on to the endoplasmic reticulum, which packages them and ships them out of the cell.
A bacterium uses its Golgi apparatus to package the proteins that its endoplasmic reticulum has made.
The Golgi apparatus digests the cell's waste, because it is drawn as a stack of flattened sacs near the edge where rubbish would collect.

units.subject: biology
units.decision_hinge: Explain why mitochondria are linked to energy supply in a cell.
units.mechanism: Mitochondria supply energy for most cellular activities by cellular respiration; the released energy is stored as ATP, and cristae increase surface area for the reactions involved.

mx.cwo: Energy released inside the mitochondrion is stored as glucose, which the cell then uses for its activities.
Mitochondria produce energy by themselves, so a cell that has had no food still has its mitochondria making energy for it.
One giant mitochondrion would release more energy than many small folded ones, because a bigger organelle has more room inside for the reactions.
Mature red blood cells have the most mitochondria of any human cell, since their whole job is to carry oxygen for respiration.
Mitochondria trap sunlight to make energy, which is why cells kept in the dark run short of energy.

units.subject: biology
units.decision_hinge: Choose the correct plastid type from the pigment or storage role being described.
units.mechanism: Plant cells use different plastids for different roles: chloroplasts contain chlorophyll for photosynthesis, chromoplasts contain non-green pigments that give colours to flowers and fruits, and leucoplasts are colourless plastids that store food materials.

mx.cwo: The red colour of a ripe tomato comes from chloroplasts that contain red chlorophyll instead of green chlorophyll.
A green frog and a green leaf are green for the same reason, because both of them contain chloroplasts full of chlorophyll.
Leucoplasts release the energy held in stored starch, which is why colourless plastids are found wherever food is stored.

units.subject: biology
units.decision_hinge: Decide how vacuoles contribute to storage and support in plant and animal cells.
units.mechanism: A mature plant cell usually has one large central vacuole filled with cell sap for storing water, minerals, and other substances, while animal-cell vacuoles may be present but are not as large and mainly help with temporary storage.

mx.cwo: The large central vacuole is filled with cytoplasm, and it is this cytoplasm that keeps the plant cell firm.
Every plant cell has one large central vacuole, including the small dividing cells at a root tip.
Animal cells contain no vacuoles at all, because the vacuole is a plant feature only.
The central vacuole pumps water into itself from outside to keep the plant cell firm and stops pumping when the plant wilts.

units.subject: biology
units.decision_hinge: Decide whether a synthetic biology example made a whole new cell from scratch or changed an existing cell using synthetic DNA.
units.mechanism: In the described synthetic biology work, only the DNA was synthetic; the cytoplasm, cell membrane, and other cell parts came from an already existing living cell.

mx.cwo: The team took the nucleus out of the recipient bacterium and put the synthetic DNA in its place.
Only the synthetic DNA was needed; once it was made, it grew into a living cell on its own in the nutrient solution.
Since synthetic DNA worked in that bacterium, scientists can now build any organism from chemicals, including a synthetic mouse.
This experiment disproves cell theory, because the new cell did not come from a pre-existing cell.

units.subject: biology
units.decision_hinge: Explain why cell division is needed for growth, repair, replacement, and reproduction.
units.mechanism: Cell division forms new cells from pre-existing cells, allowing organisms to grow, repair damaged tissues, replace worn-out cells, and reproduce.

mx.cwo: New skin cells at a wound are made directly out of the food and blood that reach the injured area.
All cells in the body divide continuously, so the nerve cells in the brain are replaced every few days just like skin cells.
A cut in the skin heals by meiosis, because meiosis is the process that makes the new cells the body needs.

units.subject: biology
units.decision_hinge: Choose mitosis or meiosis from the cell type, purpose, and daughter-cell outcome.
units.mechanism: Mitosis produces two genetically identical daughter cells with the same DNA and chromosome number as the parent cell, while meiosis produces gametes in reproductive organs and creates variation for sexual reproduction.

mx.cwo: Meiosis takes place in the reproductive organs and produces zygotes that have half the chromosome number of the parent.
Meiosis happens in any cell that needs to produce variation, so skin cells sometimes divide by meiosis to make the body varied.
Mitosis produces daughter cells that differ from the parent, while meiosis makes exact copies for growth and repair.
A human sperm cell contains 46 chromosomes, because every cell division gives the daughter cells the same number as the parent.
A bacterium reproduces by meiosis, because meiosis is the division used whenever new individuals are produced.

units.subject: biology
units.decision_hinge: Predict the consequence when normal control of cell growth, division, or death breaks down.
units.mechanism: Normal cells grow, divide, stay in place, perform their functions, and die in controlled ways; errors in mitosis or meiosis and loss of growth control can cause tumours, abnormal chromosome numbers, genetic disorders, pregnancy loss, reduced fertility, or cancer.

mx.cwo: Every tumour is cancer, because a tumour is just what the word cancer means.
An error during mitosis in a skin cell causes a genetic disorder in that person's children.
One mistake during division in one skin cell means the person already has cancer.
If a lump can be seen and felt it is cancer, and if nothing can be seen then nothing has gone wrong with the cells.
A tumour forms because the body cells there started dividing by meiosis instead of mitosis.

units.subject: biology
units.decision_hinge: Decide whether mitochondria and plastids have any genetic machinery of their own.
units.mechanism: Mitochondria and plastids both have their own DNA and ribosomes, so they can make some of their own proteins and share features with certain bacteria.

mx.cwo: Mitochondria have their own small nucleus, and that is why they can make some of their own proteins.
Mitochondria and plastids make all of their own proteins and do not depend on the rest of the cell at all.
Every organelle has its own DNA and ribosomes, so lysosomes and the Golgi apparatus make their own proteins too.
A mitochondrion is a prokaryotic cell living inside our cells, so a human cell is really a colony of separate organisms.

units.subject: biology
units.decision_hinge: Decide whether a biological structure should be treated as a tissue by checking if similar cells work together for a specific function.
units.mechanism: A tissue is a group of similar cells that work together to perform a specific function; in multicellular organisms, cells form tissues and tissues coordinate to support life processes.

mx.cwo: The heart is a tissue, because it is a group of parts that work together to carry out one specific function.
The blood, the vessel wall and the nerve running beside it form one tissue, because they all work together for circulation.
Plants have cells but not tissues, because tissues belong to animals that have organs and organ systems.
Bone counts as a tissue because it looks the same all through, but blood does not, since a liquid has no uniform structure.

units.subject: biology
units.decision_hinge: Decide why plant tissues and animal tissues differ by linking each organism's way of living and nutrition to the tissue roles it needs.
units.mechanism: Plant and animal tissues differ because plants are mostly fixed in one place and make use of available substances, while animals move, obtain food from different sources, digest it, and coordinate movement and messages.

mx.cwo: Plants need digestive tissue in the root to break down the food they absorb from the soil, just as animals digest what they eat.
Plants need muscle tissue in their stems to bend towards the light, in the same way animals need muscle to move.
Plants stay in one place because they have no muscle tissue; if a plant were given muscles it would walk about looking for food.

units.subject: biology
units.decision_hinge: Use root and shoot tip evidence to decide where increase in plant length occurs.
units.mechanism: Roots and shoots grow in length from their tips because the tips contain actively dividing cells called apical meristems; when root tips are cut, root length stops increasing.

mx.cwo: Roots grow longer because the lateral meristem along their sides keeps adding new cells all the way down.
Cutting off the root tip stops the root from getting thicker as well as from getting longer.
A tree trunk becomes thicker because the shoot tip keeps dividing and pushes the extra cells down along the sides.
The tip is white and soft, so that is where the root grows; once a root has turned brown and firm it has stopped growing anywhere.

units.subject: biology
units.decision_hinge: Choose the correct meristem type when a plant increases in length, increases in girth, or regrows after cutting or grazing.
units.mechanism: Apical meristem at root and shoot tips increases length, lateral meristem along the circumference of the stem increases girth, and intercalary meristem helps regrowth after cutting or grazing.

mx.cwo: Grass regrows after mowing because of its lateral meristem, which adds cells around the circumference of the stem.
Once the shoot tip has been cut off the plant can never grow again in any direction.
A grass blade has a pointed end, so that is its tip and grass regrows from the pointed end after it has been cut off.

units.subject: biology
units.decision_hinge: Distinguish meristematic tissue from permanent tissue by whether cells retain the ability to divide and by their cell features.
units.mechanism: Meristematic tissue contains small, tightly packed cells with thin walls, dense cytoplasm, a large nucleus, and little or no vacuole; these cells divide continuously, while cells that lose the ability to divide become specialised permanent tissues.

mx.cwo: Cells become specialised permanent tissue by dividing over and over until they have changed shape enough.
A cell with a large nucleus and dense cytoplasm is meristematic even if it has permanently stopped dividing.
Bone is animal permanent tissue and blood is animal meristematic tissue, because blood cells are still being made.
A permanent parenchyma cell in a leaf starts dividing again whenever the plant needs repair, because plant cells can always go back to being unspecialised.

units.subject: biology
units.decision_hinge: Select epidermis or dermal tissue when the plant task is protection, reducing water loss, or root absorption.
units.mechanism: The epidermis is the outermost, tightly packed single layer of plant cells that protects plant parts; its waxy covering reduces water loss, and root hair from epidermal cells increases surface area for absorption.

mx.cwo: Water enters the plant through the root cap, which pushes into the soil and takes the water in as it goes.
The epidermis of a leaf is several cell layers thick, and that thickness is what stops water escaping from the leaf.
Only leaves and stems have an epidermis, since a root is underground and does not need protection from injury.
A shiny leaf has a waxy epidermis, but a dull leaf has none and so cannot control its water loss.
Root hairs are the open ends of the xylem tubes, which reach out of the root and suck water directly from the soil.

units.subject: biology
units.decision_hinge: Choose among parenchyma, collenchyma, and sclerenchyma from a plant part's storage, flexibility, or hardness requirement.
units.mechanism: Parenchyma has living thin-walled loosely packed cells mainly for food storage and sometimes photosynthesis; collenchyma has living cells with uneven pectin-thickened corners for flexible support; sclerenchyma has thick lignified mostly dead cells for hard strength.

mx.cwo: The corners of collenchyma cells are thickened with lignin, and that lignin is what lets a young stem bend without breaking.
A nut shell could be made of parenchyma with extra thick walls, since whether the cells are alive makes no difference to how hard the shell is.
Only trees contain sclerenchyma, so a coconut shell must be parenchyma that has hardened by drying out.
A firm stem is sclerenchyma and a soft one is parenchyma, whatever the cell walls are actually made of.

units.subject: biology
units.decision_hinge: Decide whether xylem or phloem is responsible for a plant transport function or transport failure.
units.mechanism: Xylem transports water and minerals, while phloem transports food; together they form complex vascular conducting tissues because different cell types work together.

mx.cwo: Food made in the leaves travels down to the roots through the xylem.
A vascular bundle has both tissues, so whichever one lies nearer the leaf is the one that carries the food.
Water taken in by the leaves from the air travels down the xylem to the roots, where it is stored for the plant to use.
Water reaches the top of a moss through its xylem, because every plant has xylem to move water upward.
The sap from this cut stem is thin and watery, so the cut has gone through xylem; a sticky sap would mean phloem.

units.subject: biology
units.decision_hinge: Map plant tissues into dermal, ground, and vascular tissue systems instead of treating each tissue as isolated.
units.mechanism: Plant tissues are organised into tissue systems: dermal tissue forms the outer protective covering, ground tissue forms the main body between dermal and conducting tissues, and vascular tissue contains xylem and phloem for conduction.

mx.cwo: Parenchyma and collenchyma belong to the vascular tissue system, because they lie inside the stem near the conducting tubes.
A root shows only the dermal system, because the ground and vascular systems belong to the stem and the leaf.
Whatever tissue is drawn at the outside edge of the section is dermal tissue, so the outer ring of a woody stem is epidermis.

units.subject: biology
units.decision_hinge: Choose the epithelial tissue feature that fits exchange, protection, absorption, secretion, or movement.
units.mechanism: Epithelial tissue covers the body and lines internal organs; its different structures are adapted to different functions, so thin flat single layers allow rapid diffusion while protective epithelium uses multiple layers.

mx.cwo: The lining of the lung air sacs is stratified squamous epithelium, many layers thick, so that the delicate lungs are protected.
Skin is epithelium and the air sac lining is epithelium, so a piece of skin could line the air sacs and work just as well.
A thicker lining would let oxygen through faster, because there is more tissue there to take the oxygen up.
Every epithelium in the body should be many cells thick, because a single layer of cells would tear apart.
The lining of the intestine is connective tissue, because it connects the gut cavity to the blood vessels that take the food away.

units.subject: biology
units.decision_hinge: Identify connective tissue from whether the body part transports, connects, supports, protects, cushions, or transmits force.
units.mechanism: Connective tissues connect and support other tissues; blood transports materials and clots, bone gives rigid strength and protection, cartilage gives flexibility and cushioning, and tendons transmit force from muscle to bone.

mx.cwo: A tendon joins one bone to another bone across a joint and holds the two ends together.
Cartilage is bone that has not hardened yet, so a person's ears and nose turn into bone as they grow older.
The tendon carries the pull from the bone back to the muscle, which is how the muscle is told to contract.
Blood is not a connective tissue, because a liquid cannot join or support anything in the body.
A tendon is a kind of muscle, since it is the part that pulls on the bone when you lift something.

units.subject: biology
units.decision_hinge: Classify muscle tissue from whether the movement is voluntary or involuntary, and from its location and movement pattern.
units.mechanism: Skeletal muscle carries out voluntary movements such as running, writing, or lifting; smooth muscle in organs such as the stomach and intestines carries out slow continuous involuntary movements; cardiac muscle is found only in the heart and works rhythmically without fatigue.

mx.cwo: Food is moved along the intestine by cardiac muscle, which works rhythmically without ever getting tired.
Cardiac muscle is found in the heart and also in the intestine and the blood vessels, wherever movement must go on without rest.
Since muscles are under our control, a person can slow their own heartbeat and stop their intestines moving just by deciding to.
Cardiac muscle has stripes like skeletal muscle, so the heart must be under voluntary control too.
Smooth muscle in the intestine works without conscious control because it has no nerve supply reaching it at all.

units.subject: biology
units.decision_hinge: Use neuron structure to explain how the body senses, communicates, and responds.

units.decision_hinge: Decide whether a unicellular organism is reproducing by binary fission or multiple fission.

units.decision_hinge: Decide whether regeneration is the same as normal reproduction.

mx.cwo: A Planaria cut into several pieces that each become a worm is fragmentation, since the body has broken into fragments.
Even a dead piece of Planaria tissue will grow into a whole worm if it is kept in water long enough.

units.subject: biology
units.decision_hinge: Decide when a plant part can produce a new plant by vegetative propagation.

units.subject: biology

units.decision_hinge: Decide whether a reproductive mode is asexual or sexual from the number of individuals involved.

units.subject: biology
units.decision_hinge: Decide why sexual reproduction cannot simply combine full DNA copies from two parents every generation.

Germ-cells solve the doubling problem by not copying their DNA at all, so no new DNA is made before fertilisation.

units.subject: biology

units.subject: biology
units.decision_hinge: Decide whether puberty changes show only general growth or sexual maturation.

The grass leaf rule also covers this: Do not label every epidermal cell in a grass leaf as bulliform, so it is not an exception.

The answer is grass leaf because of the most obvious label, colour, size or printed number in the stem, without using 'Identify bulliform cells by their position and cellular appearance in' as the operative test.

units.subject: biology
units.decision_hinge: Distinguish a tissue, an organ, and an organ system by their level in the biological hierarchy.
units.mechanism: Cells and intercellular substances form tissues, tissues combine in specific proportions and patterns to form organs, and organs associate to form organ systems that divide the work needed for the whole body to survive.

mx.cwo: The frog's digestive system is an organ, because it is the one part of the body that does digestion.
A lump containing muscle cells and nerve cells mixed at random is an organ, because an organ is just tissues put together.
Organ systems join together to form organs, and organs join together to form tissues, so a tissue is the largest structure in the frog's body.
In Amoeba the food vacuole is the digestive organ and the cell membrane is the excretory organ system.
The stomach is an organ system because it is big, and the thin lining inside it is a tissue because it is small.

units.subject: biology
units.decision_hinge: Classify the frog as an amphibian and as a poikilotherm using habitat and body-temperature evidence.
units.mechanism: A frog lives on land and in freshwater and belongs to class Amphibia; its body temperature varies with environmental temperature, so it is cold-blooded or poikilothermic.

mx.cwo: Rana tigrina belongs to class Reptilia, because it is a cold-blooded animal that crawls on land.
A duck is a poikilotherm because it lives both on land and in freshwater, just like the frog.
The frog is warm-blooded because its temperature changes with the pond, and a dog is cold-blooded because its temperature stays at 37 degrees Celsius.
Crocodiles and water snakes are amphibians, because they live both on land and in freshwater.
An earthworm is an amphibian because its skin is moist and slippery like a frog's skin.

units.subject: biology
units.decision_hinge: Infer the function of a frog's external feature from its structure instead of identifying the feature by position alone.
units.mechanism: External frog structures support particular functions: mucus keeps the skin smooth, slippery, and moist; the nictitating membrane protects the bulging eyes; large muscular hind limbs support locomotion; and webbed digits aid swimming.

mx.cwo: The nictitating membrane keeps the frog's skin moist and slippery, while mucus covers and protects the bulging eyes.
The frog swims because its hind limbs are large and muscular; the webbing between the digits makes no difference to swimming.
The nictitating membrane and the mucus are both swimming aids, because every outside feature of a frog helps it move through water.
The hind limbs are the biggest limbs, so they catch the food, and the small fore limbs are used for swimming.
The mucous glands are the frog's breathing organs: they take oxygen from the air and pass it into the blood.

units.subject: biology
units.decision_hinge: Connect the frog's carnivorous diet to its short alimentary canal and place capture and stomach digestion at their correct stages.
units.mechanism: The frog's digestive system contains an alimentary canal and digestive glands; because the frog is carnivorous, the canal is short and the intestine is reduced, while captured food is acted on by hydrochloric acid and gastric juices in the stomach to form chyme.

mx.cwo: The liver and pancreas are parts of the frog's alimentary canal, so its digestive system is just one long tube.
A frog's alimentary canal is short because a frog is a small animal; a plant-eating frog of the same size would have exactly the same short canal.
The frog eats insects, so its intestine is long, because meat needs a longer canal to be broken down.
Hydrochloric acid works all the way along the frog's gut, so the food in the duodenum and intestine is still being digested by acid.
Food goes from the mouth into the duodenum first and then back into the stomach, where it is finally turned into chyme.

units.subject: biology
units.decision_hinge: Select cutaneous diffusion through moist skin as the frog's respiratory mechanism in water.
units.mechanism: In water, the frog's moist, highly vascularised skin acts as the aquatic respiratory organ, and dissolved oxygen is exchanged through it by diffusion.

mx.cwo: The frog's skin pumps dissolved oxygen into the blood by active transport, using energy supplied by the blood vessels.
A frog with completely dry skin can still take in oxygen through it in water, because the skin is full of blood vessels.
In water the frog gives out oxygen through its skin and takes in carbon dioxide, because pond water already contains plenty of oxygen.
On land the frog also breathes only through its skin, so its lungs play no part in respiration at any time.

units.subject: biology
units.decision_hinge: Distinguish the closed blood vascular system from the accompanying lymphatic system by their components.
units.mechanism: The frog has a well-developed closed blood vascular system made up of the heart, blood vessels, and blood, and it also has a lymphatic system made up of lymph and lymph channels.

mx.cwo: The frog's lymphatic system is made up of lymph, the heart and the blood vessels.
The frog's blood vascular system is open, because blood leaves the vessels and turns into lymph in the lymph channels.
The lymphatic system is a closed system too, with its own heart pumping lymph round a complete circuit.
The colourless fluid inside the frog's heart is lymph, and only the red fluid in the vessels counts as blood.

units.subject: biology
units.decision_hinge: Identify the frog as ureotelic and distinguish the organs that eliminate nitrogenous waste from nearby digestive and reproductive structures.
units.mechanism: The frog's excretory system contains a pair of kidneys, ureters, a urinary bladder, and the cloaca, and the frog is ureotelic because it excretes urea.

mx.cwo: The frog is uricotelic, because the nitrogenous waste removed by its kidneys is uric acid.
Any animal with a pair of kidneys, ureters and a urinary bladder is ureotelic, so a pigeon is ureotelic as well.
Every animal excretes urea, so insects and freshwater fishes are ureotelic like the frog.
The gall bladder is an excretory organ, because it is a thin-walled sac holding fluid just like the urinary bladder.
Ureotelic means the animal excretes through its ureters, so an animal without ureters cannot be ureotelic.

units.subject: biology
units.decision_hinge: Map each sensory function to the correct frog receptor organ while keeping neural and endocrine coordination distinct.
units.mechanism: Control and coordination in the frog include neural and endocrine systems; endocrine glands secrete hormones, while sensory papillae, taste buds, nasal epithelium, eyes, and the tympanum with internal ears serve touch, taste, smell, vision, and hearing respectively.

mx.cwo: Touch in the frog is received by the taste buds, and taste is received by the sensory papillae.
The tympanum by itself is the frog's hearing organ, and the internal ears take no part in hearing.
Hormones travel along the frog's nerves from the endocrine glands, so the endocrine system is one part of the neural system.
All five senses are received by the sensory papillae, because those are the parts actually called sensory.

units.subject: biology
units.decision_hinge: Distinguish male and female frog reproductive organisation by whether the gonads connect functionally with the kidneys and by the ducts shown with each system.
units.mechanism: Male testes are attached near the upper kidneys and the male reproductive route communicates with a urinogenital duct that opens into the cloaca, whereas female ovaries lie near the kidneys without a functional connection to them and are associated with oviducts.

mx.cwo: The female frog releases her ova through a urinogenital duct, while the male's sperm travel along oviducts to the cloaca.
The female frog's ovaries are joined to her kidneys, so the ova pass into the ureters before reaching the cloaca.
The testes are part of the excretory system, because they are attached to the upper part of the kidneys.
Sperm leave the male frog through the ureters and collect in the urinary bladder before passing out at the cloaca.

units.subject: biology
units.decision_hinge: Recognise the cloaca as a shared chamber for digestive, urinary, and male reproductive outputs rather than assigning it to only one system.
units.mechanism: The cloaca is a small median chamber through which faecal matter, urine, and sperm pass to the exterior.

mx.cwo: Faecal matter reaches the cloaca from the urinary bladder, and urine reaches it from the rectum.
Because faeces, urine and sperm all pass through the cloaca, the digestive, excretory and reproductive systems are one single system in the frog.
The urinary bladder is a shared chamber as well, so faecal matter is stored in it along with urine.
The frog has only one opening at the back, so there is a single tube running from its mouth to that opening.

units.subject: biology
units.decision_hinge: Explain the frog's benefit to crops and ecosystems through its feeding role and position in food chains and food webs.
units.mechanism: Frogs benefit people by eating insects and thereby protecting crops, and they help maintain ecological balance as an important link in food chains and food webs.

mx.cwo: The frog is a producer in the food chain, so it protects the crop by making food for the crop plants.
Frogs protect crops just by living in the field, whether or not they eat any insects there.
Insects feed on frogs, so a field with more frogs will have more insects in it and more crop damage.
Frogs protect crops by eating everything in the field, including worms and young plant shoots, because any feeding by a frog helps the crop.

units.subject: biology
units.decision_hinge: Decide whether a biological structure is a complete cell by asking whether it can support independent existence and the essential functions of life.
units.mechanism: A complete cell is the smallest organisation that can ensure independent living; a structure smaller than a complete cell cannot do so by itself.

mx.cwo: A leaf cell is not a complete cell, because it cannot move about by itself the way Amoeba can.
A mango tree is one complete cell, because it exists independently and carries out all the essential functions of life.
A liver cell is not really a cell at all, because it dies when it is taken out of the body and cannot live on its own.
Anything small enough to need a microscope is a cell, so a ribosome seen under an electron microscope is a cell.

units.subject: biology
units.decision_hinge: Use both parts of cell theory when judging claims about the cellular composition and origin of living organisms.
units.mechanism: All living organisms are composed of cells and products of cells, and every new cell arises from a pre-existing cell.

mx.cwo: Virchow proposed that all organisms are composed of cells, and Schleiden and Schwann explained that new cells arise from pre-existing cells.
Cell theory says organisms are made only of cells, so bone matrix and hair are not covered by cell theory at all.
New cells are built up by the body out of food materials, so a wound heals when the flesh and fluid there turn into new cells.
Schleiden and Schwann's cell theory already stated that every cell arises from a pre-existing cell, so nothing needed to be added later.

units.subject: biology
units.decision_hinge: Treat size and shape as variable cell features rather than as tests of whether a structure is a cell.
units.mechanism: Cells can differ greatly in size, shape and activity while remaining cells.

mx.cwo: Mycoplasma is the largest isolated single cell, and an ostrich egg is about 0.3 micrometres long.
The whole ostrich egg, shell and white included, is one single cell about 15 centimetres across.
All human cells are about 7.0 micrometres across, because that is the size of a human red blood cell.
An ostrich egg is a product of cells and not a cell, because it is stored food material made by the hen's body.

units.subject: biology
units.decision_hinge: Classify a cell as prokaryotic or eukaryotic from the organisation of its nucleus and membrane-bound organelles.
units.mechanism: Prokaryotic cells lack a well-defined membrane-bound nucleus and membrane-bound organelles, whereas eukaryotic cells have a nucleus and extensive cytoplasmic compartmentalisation by membrane-bound organelles.

mx.cwo: A bacterium has no genetic material at all, which is why it has no nucleus and cannot pass on characters.
A bacterium is eukaryotic, because its DNA is gathered in one region of the cell and that region is its nucleus.
A cell with a nucleus and membrane-bound organelles is prokaryotic, and a cell lacking both is eukaryotic.
Yeast and Amoeba are prokaryotes, because they are microscopic single-celled organisms like bacteria.
Blue-green algae are eukaryotic plant cells, because they are green and make their own food by photosynthesis.
Bacteria are eukaryotic, because they contain ribosomes and ribosomes are membrane-bound organelles.

units.subject: biology
units.decision_hinge: Distinguish structures shared across cell types from structures characteristic of plant or animal cells.
units.mechanism: Ribosomes occur in both prokaryotic and eukaryotic cells, while a cell wall, plastids and a large central vacuole distinguish typical plant cells from animal cells, and a centrosome is characteristic of animal cells.

mx.cwo: Animal cells have a cell wall as well; the difference is that plant cells have a plasma membrane instead of one.
Every eukaryotic cell contains a cell wall, plastids, a large central vacuole and a centrosome.
A cell wall, plastids and a large central vacuole mark an animal cell, while a plant cell is recognised by its centrosome.
A bacterium is a plant cell, because it has a cell wall around its plasma membrane.

units.subject: biology
units.decision_hinge: Identify the layers of a bacterial cell envelope in outside-to-inside order and apply the Mycoplasma exception to the cell wall.
units.mechanism: A typical bacterial cell envelope is organised as glycocalyx, cell wall and plasma membrane from outside to inside, but Mycoplasma lacks the cell wall.

mx.cwo: From outside inwards the bacterial envelope is capsule, then slime layer, then cell wall, then plasma membrane.
Every bacterium has a thick tough capsule outside its cell wall, so a bacterium with only a loose slime layer has no glycocalyx.
A plant cell has a glycocalyx outside its cell wall, and then the plasma membrane inside the wall.
The cell wall is the outermost layer of a bacterium, with the glycocalyx and the plasma membrane inside it.
Mycoplasma has no glycocalyx, but it still has a cell wall and a plasma membrane.

units.subject: biology
units.decision_hinge: Recognise a mesosome as an inward extension of the prokaryotic plasma membrane and connect that structure to its stated cellular roles.
units.mechanism: A mesosome consists of plasma-membrane infoldings in the form of vesicles, tubules and lamellae that increase membrane surface and participate in several prokaryotic processes.

mx.cwo: A mesosome is formed by infoldings of the bacterial cell wall reaching into the cytoplasm.
A mesosome carries out DNA replication and respiration by itself, and its infolding has nothing to do with the membrane surface available.
A mesosome is formed where the plasma membrane pushes outward from the cell surface, so mesosomes stick out of the bacterium.
The mesosomes of a plant cell are the infoldings of its plasma membrane that carry out respiration and secretion.
The mesosome is the bacterium's mitochondrion, and its cristae carry out respiration inside its double membrane.

units.subject: biology
units.decision_hinge: Use bacterial flagella, pili and fimbriae for the correct surface-function inference instead of treating every projection as a motility structure.
units.mechanism: Bacterial flagella are filamentous surface extensions associated with motility, whereas pili and fimbriae are bacterial surface structures that do not perform motility.

mx.cwo: Pili are the small bristle-like structures on the bacterium and fimbriae are the elongated tubular ones.
Every bacterium swims, because a bacterial cell always carries thin filamentous flagella extending from its cell wall.
Flagella hold the bacterium onto a surface, and it is the pili that push the cell through the water.
A bacterium covered in many bristles is the fastest swimmer, because more projections mean more pushing.
A bacterial flagellum is an outgrowth covered by plasma membrane containing nine pairs of microtubules and a central pair.

units.subject: biology
units.decision_hinge: Classify a ribosome from its sedimentation class and subunits without adding the subunit values arithmetically.
units.mechanism: Prokaryotic 70S ribosomes contain 50S and 30S subunits, whereas eukaryotic 80S ribosomes contain 60S and 40S subunits; ribosomes are non-membrane-bound RNA-protein particles.

mx.cwo: A bacterial ribosome is 80S with 60S and 40S subunits, while a human cytoplasmic ribosome is 70S.
A ribosome inside a mitochondrion is membrane-bound, because it is enclosed within a membrane-bound organelle.
The ribosomes inside chloroplasts and mitochondria are 80S, because those organelles lie inside eukaryotic cells.
A 60S subunit belongs to a 70S ribosome, because 60 is nearer to 70 than it is to 80.
A 70S ribosome is built from a 50S subunit and a 40S subunit.

units.subject: biology
units.decision_hinge: Infer plasma-membrane behaviour from the phospholipid bilayer, protein placement and fluid mosaic organisation.
units.mechanism: The plasma membrane is a selectively permeable, quasi-fluid phospholipid bilayer containing surface-associated peripheral proteins and partially or fully buried integral proteins.

mx.cwo: The plasma membrane is a bilayer of protein with phospholipid molecules scattered inside it.
The proteins in the membrane are fixed in position, so a cell cannot form new junctions or take material in by endocytosis.
Because the membrane is selectively permeable, every molecule in the cytoplasm can cross it freely whenever the cell needs it to.
There are open gaps between the phospholipids of the membrane, because the diagram shows separate balls with spaces between them.

units.subject: biology
units.decision_hinge: Distinguish the plant or fungal cell wall from the plasma membrane and identify how neighbouring plant cells are joined and connected.
units.mechanism: The non-living rigid cell wall lies outside the plasma membrane in plants and fungi, while the calcium-pectate middle lamella glues neighbouring cells and plasmodesmata connect their cytoplasm.

mx.cwo: The middle lamella is made of cellulose while the plant cell wall is made of calcium pectate.
Plasmodesmata lie on the outer surface of the cell wall and join the walls of neighbouring cells to each other.
In a plant cell the plasma membrane lies outside the cell wall, so the wall is the innermost layer next to the cytoplasm.
Neighbouring animal cells are glued by a middle lamella of calcium pectate and connected through plasmodesmata.

units.subject: biology
units.decision_hinge: Group organelles into the endomembrane system by coordinated function rather than merely by the presence of a membrane.
units.mechanism: The endoplasmic reticulum, Golgi complex, lysosomes and vacuoles form the endomembrane system because their functions are coordinated even though their structures and individual functions are distinct.

mx.cwo: The endomembrane system consists of the endoplasmic reticulum, the Golgi complex, ribosomes and vacuoles.
The vacuole is not part of the endomembrane system, because its structure and its individual function are quite different from those of the ER and the Golgi.
The ER, the Golgi complex, lysosomes and vacuoles all carry out the same function, because they belong to one system.

units.subject: biology
units.decision_hinge: Choose rough or smooth endoplasmic reticulum from ribosome attachment and the material being synthesised.
units.mechanism: Rough endoplasmic reticulum bears surface ribosomes and is prominent in cells active in protein synthesis and secretion, whereas smooth endoplasmic reticulum lacks surface ribosomes and is a major site of lipid synthesis.

mx.cwo: Rough ER is rough because lysosomes are attached all over its surface.
Smooth ER makes steroidal hormones in every cell, so a plant leaf cell makes steroid hormones on its smooth ER.
All the protein in a cell is made on rough ER, so a bacterium with no ER makes no protein at all.
A cell in rough dry skin has rough ER, and a cell in smooth moist lining has smooth ER.
Rough ER is part of the nuclear envelope, so protein synthesis and secretion take place inside the nucleus.

units.subject: biology
units.decision_hinge: Relate Golgi polarity and packaging to material delivery and lysosome formation.
units.mechanism: The Golgi apparatus is a polar stack of interconnected cisternae with distinct cis and trans faces that packages materials for intracellular delivery or secretion and produces lysosomal vesicles through packaging.

mx.cwo: The Golgi apparatus packages hydrolytic enzymes into ribosomes and releases them into the cytoplasm.
A lysosome is a vesicle of packaged material with no enzymes in it, so it only stores what the Golgi sends.
Everything the Golgi packages is secreted outside the cell, so a lysosome must leave the cell as soon as it forms.
The face drawn at the top of the Golgi stack is the cis face, whichever side of the picture the ER is on.
The Golgi complex makes the proteins on its own cisternae and then sends them out, so the ER plays no part in secretion.

units.subject: biology
units.decision_hinge: Infer a vacuole's role from its membrane, contents and cellular context.
units.mechanism: A vacuole is a cytoplasmic space bounded by the tonoplast, and its function depends on context: storage and concentration of materials in plant cells, osmoregulation and excretion in Amoeba, or temporary enclosure of engulfed food in many protists.

mx.cwo: The contractile vacuole of Amoeba forms by engulfing food particles, while the food vacuole of a protist controls water balance.
The ion concentration inside a plant vacuole is lower than in the cytoplasm, because materials only leak slowly across the tonoplast.
Only plant cells have vacuoles, so the contractile space in an Amoeba is not a vacuole at all.
Any large clear space inside or between cells is a storage vacuole, so the air space between two leaf cells is a vacuole too.
A food vacuole in a protist is a lysosome, because it is a membrane-bound sac formed by the Golgi to digest material.

units.subject: biology
units.decision_hinge: Distinguish a mitochondrion from a chloroplast by the organisation of its two membranes and internal compartments.
units.mechanism: A mitochondrion has an outer membrane and an inner membrane folded into cristae around an inner compartment, whereas a chloroplast has a double envelope surrounding stroma that contains thylakoids organised into grana and linked by stroma lamellae.

mx.cwo: A mitochondrion has an outer and an inner membrane that are both smooth, so its matrix is one plain space with no folds in it.
The grana enclose the stroma, so the stroma is the space held inside a stack of thylakoids.
An animal cell contains chloroplasts as well as mitochondria, because both are double-membrane organelles of the cytoplasm.
A green organelle is a chloroplast and a colourless one is a mitochondrion, so a chloroplast kept in the dark turns into a mitochondrion.

units.subject: biology
units.decision_hinge: Distinguish the cytoskeleton, cilia or flagella, and centrioles by their organisation and role.
units.mechanism: The cytoskeleton is a cytoplasmic network of microtubules, microfilaments and intermediate filaments; eukaryotic cilia and flagella are membrane-covered outgrowths with a microtubular axoneme; a centriole is a cylinder built from nine peripheral triplet fibrils.

mx.cwo: A cilium is a bare bundle of microtubules sticking out of the cell with no membrane over it.
The cytoskeleton is the bundle of microtubules inside a cilium, so a cell with no cilia has no cytoskeleton.
A cilium is a thin filament growing out of the cell wall, with no microtubules inside it at all.

units.subject: biology
units.decision_hinge: Relate the diffuse chromatin of an interphase nucleus to the distinct chromosomes seen during cell division.
units.mechanism: In interphase, nuclear genetic material appears as a loose, indistinct chromatin network in the nucleoplasm; during cell division, it appears as structured chromosomes.

mx.cwo: During cell division the nuclear material appears as a loose network of chromatin, and in interphase it appears as distinct chromosomes.
The nucleolus is a membrane-bound organelle inside the nucleus, kept separate from the nucleoplasm by its own membrane.
At division the nucleolus condenses into a chromosome as well, so a cell with two nucleoli forms two extra chromosomes.
An interphase cell has no chromosomes, only a network, so no chromosome number can be given for it.

units.subject: biology
units.decision_hinge: Classify chromosome form from the position of the primary constriction and keep a secondary constriction distinct from the centromere.
units.mechanism: The centromere is the primary constriction that joins chromatids and determines chromosome arm proportions, while a secondary constriction at a constant location may separate a satellite.

mx.cwo: Any narrow point anywhere along a chromosome is a secondary constriction, with a satellite lying beyond it.
A chromosome whose centromere lies exactly in the middle has two arms of unequal length, so it is acrocentric.
Every chromosome has two arms of equal length, because the centromere holds the chromatids together at their middle.
The pale non-staining gap is the centromere, because the centromere is the part of the chromosome that does not take up stain.
This chromosome is metacentric because its two chromatids are of equal length.

units.subject: biology
units.decision_hinge: Decide whether an analysis result describes the elements in living tissue or the compounds and functional groups present in it.
units.mechanism: Elemental analysis reports elements such as hydrogen, oxygen, chlorine, and carbon, whereas compound analysis requires extraction and chemical tests that reveal organic and inorganic constituents and functional groups.

mx.cwo: An aldehyde group was detected, so the compound present in the tissue is aldehyde.
Sodium and chlorine were found in the tissue, so the tissue contains NaCl.
Carbon, hydrogen and oxygen were found in the tissue, so the molecular formula of the tissue material is CHO.
The whole tissue extract was analysed and its molecular formula is C6H12O6, so that is the compound present.

units.subject: biology
units.decision_hinge: Identify an alpha-amino acid from its amino group, acidic group, alpha-carbon, and variable R group, then classify it from its amino and carboxyl groups.
units.mechanism: An alpha-amino acid has an amino group and an acidic group attached to the same alpha-carbon; its R group distinguishes particular amino acids, while the numbers of amino and carboxyl groups distinguish acidic, basic, and neutral types.

mx.cwo: Glycine has a methyl group as its R group and alanine has hydrogen as its R group.
A molecule with an amino group at one end and a carboxyl group at the other end is an alpha-amino acid.
An amino acid with two carboxyl groups and one amino group is a basic amino acid.
Every amino acid is an acidic amino acid, because the word acid is part of its name.
Lysine is a neutral amino acid, because it has one amino group and one carboxyl group on its alpha-carbon.

units.subject: biology
units.decision_hinge: Distinguish primary metabolites with identifiable roles in normal physiology from the diverse secondary metabolites whose host functions are not all understood.
units.mechanism: Primary metabolites have identifiable functions and known roles in normal physiological processes, whereas the roles of all secondary metabolites in their host organisms are not yet understood.

mx.cwo: Secondary metabolites have no role at all in the organisms that make them, because their roles in the host are not understood.
Proteins and lipids are secondary metabolites, because they form several chemically different groups.
Chlorophyll is a secondary metabolite, because it is a coloured pigment like carotenoid and anthocyanin.

units.subject: biology
units.decision_hinge: Use acid-soluble versus acid-insoluble fractionation without mistaking every insoluble component for a high-molecular-weight polymer.
units.mechanism: The acid-soluble pool contains compounds of approximately 18 to 800 Da, while the acid-insoluble fraction contains proteins, nucleic acids, polysaccharides, and lipids; proteins, nucleic acids, and polysaccharides are polymeric macromolecules, but lipids enter this fraction because they occur in membrane structures.

mx.cwo: The acid-soluble fraction holds the proteins, nucleic acids and polysaccharides, while the acid-insoluble pool holds the molecules of 18 to 800 Da.
The acid-insoluble fraction comes only from the organelles, so no cytoplasmic molecule appears in it.
Starch belongs to the acid-soluble pool, because starch dissolves when flour is stirred into water.

units.subject: biology
units.decision_hinge: Recognise a protein as a peptide-bonded amino-acid heteropolymer rather than a homopolymer or an unlinked mixture of amino acids.
units.mechanism: A protein is a polypeptide: a linear chain of amino acids joined by peptide bonds and treated as a heteropolymer because amino acids occur in different types.

mx.cwo: The amino acids of a protein are held together by hydrogen bonds, so gentle heating separates the chain back into free amino acids.
A protein is any branched network of amino acids joined by peptide bonds, like glycogen but made of amino acids.
Starch is a heteropolymer, because every biological polymer is built from different kinds of monomer.
A chain of five amino acids is not a protein, because a protein has to be a long fibre you can see.

units.subject: biology
units.decision_hinge: Distinguish polysaccharides, nucleic acids, and proteins by the units linked in their polymer chains.
units.mechanism: Polysaccharides are long chains of sugars, nucleic acids are polynucleotides, and proteins are polypeptides made from amino acids.

mx.cwo: Nucleic acids are chains of amino acids and proteins are chains of nucleotides.
Sucrose is a polysaccharide, because a polysaccharide is any chain of sugar units joined together.
The calcium pectate of the middle lamella is a polysaccharide, because everything that forms a plant cell wall is a polysaccharide.

units.subject: biology
units.decision_hinge: Distinguish a nitrogenous base, a nucleoside, and a nucleotide by checking for sugar and phosphate attachments.
units.mechanism: A nitrogenous base attached to a sugar forms a nucleoside, and addition of a phosphate group to the base-sugar unit forms a nucleotide.

mx.cwo: Adenosine contains a base, a ribose sugar and a phosphate group, while adenylic acid is only a base joined to ribose.
Adenosine is a nucleotide, because adenine is already joined to a ribose sugar in it.
Adding a phosphate group to a nucleoside turns it into a nucleoside no longer but a nucleotide only when the phosphate is taken away again.
Glucose 6-phosphate is a nucleotide, because any molecule carrying a phosphate group is a nucleotide.
A nitrogenous base carrying a phosphate group and no sugar is a nucleotide.

units.subject: biology
units.decision_hinge: Assign primary, secondary, tertiary, and quaternary protein structure to sequence, local chain conformation, whole-chain folding, and subunit arrangement respectively.
units.mechanism: Primary structure is the amino-acid sequence of a polypeptide, secondary structure is a local conformation such as an alpha helix, tertiary structure is the folding of one polypeptide chain, and quaternary structure is the arrangement of multiple folded polypeptide subunits.

mx.cwo: The first amino acid of a polypeptide lies at its C-terminal end and the last one lies at its N-terminal end.
A single folded polypeptide chain has quaternary structure, because it has a definite three-dimensional arrangement in space.
The arrangement of several subunits is the protein's primary structure and its amino-acid sequence is its quaternary structure.
A protein made of beta sheets has no secondary structure, because secondary structure means an alpha helix.

units.subject: biology
units.decision_hinge: Recognise enzyme action by substrate binding at an active-site pocket while retaining the ribozyme exception to the usual protein identity of enzymes.
units.mechanism: Almost all enzymes are proteins whose folded structure creates an active-site crevice or pocket into which the substrate fits, but some catalytic nucleic acids are ribozymes.

mx.cwo: Protein is the label that belongs on this item, so 'Recognise enzyme action by substrate binding at an active-site pocket' is answered as protein rather than enzyme.
enzyme still holds here even though A substrate must diffuse toward and bind at the enzyme's active site before conversion is missing from the stem.

The answer is enzyme because of the most obvious label, colour, size or printed number in the stem, without using 'Recognise enzyme action by substrate binding at an active-site pocket' as the operative test.

units.subject: biology
units.decision_hinge: Calculate reaction rate as product formed per unit time and distinguish this quantitative rate from merely naming a reaction.
units.mechanism: Reaction rate is the amount of product formed per unit time, expressed as rate = delta P / delta t.

mx.cwo: Time interval is the label that belongs on this item, so 'Calculate reaction rate as product formed per unit time and' is answered as time interval rather than product amount.
Time interval is what produces product amount, so the usual direction of this relation is run backwards.

atria still holds here even though Tricuspid and bicuspid valves govern flow between atria and ventricles is missing from the stem.

joint diastole still holds here even though In joint diastole all four chambers are relaxed and the tricuspid and bicuspid valves are is missing from the stem.

units.mechanism: The P wave represents atrial depolarisation, the QRS complex represents ventricular depolarisation that initiates ventricular contraction, and the T wave represents ventricular repolarisation; QRS complexes counted over time give heart rate.

mx.cwo: P wave is the label that belongs on this item, so 'Map ECG features to the correct electrical event and use QRS counts to' is answered as P wave rather than ECG.
ECG still holds here even though The P wave is associated with excitation of the atria, not the ventricles is missing from the stem.
Heartbeat rate is what produces cardiac electrical event, so the usual direction of this relation is run backwards.
The ECG rule also covers this: Do not map P to ventricular excitation, so it is not an exception.

The answer is ECG because of the most obvious label, colour, size or printed number in the stem, without using 'Map ECG features to the correct electrical event and use QRS counts to' as the operative test.

mx.cwo: right ventricle still holds here even though The pulmonary artery begins the route from the right ventricle toward the lungs despite is missing from the stem.

Right ventricle is computed by squaring pulmonary artery and leaving right ventricle linear, so the written value is 30.

units.subject: biology
units.decision_hinge: Distinguish intrinsic initiation of cardiac activity from external moderation of that activity.

mx.cwo: Nodal tissue is the label that belongs on this item, so 'Distinguish intrinsic initiation of cardiac activity from external' is answered as nodal tissue rather than cardiac muscle.
cardiac muscle still holds here even though Myogenic regulation attributes the normal intrinsic control to specialised cardiac muscle is missing from the stem.
The cardiac muscle rule also covers this: Do not define myogenic control as control initiated by the medulla, so it is not an exception.

blood pressure still holds here even though The first value in 120/80 is the systolic pumping pressure is missing from the stem.
